newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - "Sokaiya" racketeers nurtured on Japan's dark side.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - "Sokaiya" racketeers nurtured on Japan's dark side.

text.p: Japan's elusive corporate racketeers, currently at the heart of major scandals, have long been portrayed as parasites.
In fact, according to racketeers and lawyers, many of them are nurtured by big businesses.
Known as "sokaiya", racketeers boast that they survive by being able to read the fine print on a balance sheet and claim they can ply their trade because firms actually want them around.
Sokaiya, derived from the Japanese for shareholders' meetings (kabunushi sokai), extort money from firms by threatening to pose revealing questions at such meetings.
They are now at the heart of scandals involving Japan's largest stockbroker Nomura Securities Co. Ltd. and a big foodstuff company, Ajinomoto Co. Inc..

Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki stepped down last month after an internal investigation revealed that two Nomura directors had paid at least 38 million yen ($300,000) to a real estate firm run by a relative of a sokaiya.
Prosecutors followed Sakamaki's resignation with raids on Nomura offices, but no one has yet been arrested. However, many corporate clients froze dealings with Nomura.
In the case of Ajinomoto, two employees were arrested on suspicion of paying some six million yen ($48,000) to nine sokaiya. The nine were also arrested.
FEWER BUT MORE EFFECTIVE

Before 1982, when the Commercial Code was revised to outlaw corporate payments to them, there were about 4,500 sokaiya in some 500 groups of various sizes. In the 15 years since then, they have dwindled to 250 sokaiya in about eight loose groups.
They may be fewer but are now more effective than old-timers, one sokaiya told Reuters.
"The few that survived have a high level of intelligence," said the sokaiya, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
"Many are better than some finance ministers or board members of big businesses when analysing economic and corporate indices and balance sheets," he told Reuters.
That they exist is no secret. There is even an annual publication sold by a publishing house which lists their names, and some sokaiya seem to benefit from having their names printed.
The sokaiya refused to answer what he knew specifically about the Nomura or Ajinomoto cases, but accused the Japanese media of portraying sokaiya as the sole culprits.
FIRMS THEMSELVES USING RACKETEERS

"What I want you to know is the fact that many firms, about 20 percent of the First Section firms (big firms listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange) approach us on their own initiative, not only for shareholders' meetings but as part of everyday operations," the sokaiya said.

He did not elaborate, but lawyers and police have said many firms have been known to use the "good offices" of sokaiya to cover up scandals ranging from shady property deals and illegal politicial donations to extra-marital affairs among top brass.

Some big businesses have even been accused of training up-and-coming sokaiya in balance-sheet reading, because such "teacher-student" ties will win the firm immunity in the future once the young sokaiya comes of age.
In a typical case, the paid-off or "friendly sokaiya" will use his influence to stop "enemy sokaiya" from making extortion attempts.
In most cases, however, the "friendly" and "enemy" sokaiya are actually connected behind the scenes and in effect are acting out pre-determined "sting" roles.
"The friendly and enemy sokaiya are all connected in the roots and these ties are not visible above ground," another sokaiya told a recent court hearing in Kyoto, western Japan.
GANGSTER CONNECTIONS

The first sokaiya did not say if he or his group was related to "yakuza" crime syndicates, but sokaiya often make indirect threats showing off such ties, for example, by transferring ownership of their shares to yakuza bosses.
They cannot make direct references to yakuza in extortion attempts because of recent police crackdowns on mobsters who intervene in corporate affairs.
"Not everything about us is evil. Firms are also evil," the sokaiya told Reuters in response to a question about ties with gangsters.
In the end, he said the individual investor was the victim.

"This is what might be called a money game. Since it is a game, there are winners and there are losers, but there are no draws. The end losers are the average investors on the street. This is a product of Japan's corporate and political culture."
He said this culture also enabled many politicians to get away with shady donations from big businesses.
This dark side of Japan's corporate culture means that ties between firms and sokaiya will never disappear, he said.
"In the end, like in the current cases, three or four people will be arrested and that would be the end of it," the sokaiya said.

"The only way to get rid of them is for Japanese firms to pay more dividends -- which in turn will mean the growth of more responsible investors. At present, Japanese are mostly short-term speculators who tend to ignore corporate behaviour not related to profit," lawyer Shigeru Nakajima wrote in the daily Yomiuri Shimbun.
"In addition, the firms must do away with their secrecy and make more information available to potential investors," said Nakajima. ($1=125 yen)
